I’ll check the project setup, install the missing dependencies, and verify that `npm run dev` starts.

Fixed—the project dependencies were missing. I installed them with `npm ci`.

`npm run dev` now starts successfully, and the site returns HTTP 200 at [localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). The server is running.

No source changes. npm reported 7 dependency vulnerabilities; I left dependency versions unchanged.
fix all issues next.js has raised, without modifying the ui ux of the website

I’ll check the Next.js output, dependency warnings, and project checks. I’ll fix the issues while preserving the website’s appearance and behavior.

Lint and TypeScript checks pass. The dependency audit found a fixable PostCSS issue and an unpatched issue in the Next.js lint tooling. I’ll fix PostCSS, check the production build and browser output, and leave the unpatched issue clearly reported.

The production build passes, and the production dependency audit now reports zero vulnerabilities. No UI files have changed. I’m running the desktop/mobile interaction tests and checking all four pages for browser errors.

All four pages load without browser warnings or errors. The compiled CSS is byte-for-byte identical before and after the dependency fix, and the interaction tests are passing so far.

The remaining five audit alerts trace back to one unpatched `braces` issue in development tooling. npm’s proposed fix would downgrade the Next.js lint package to a different major version.

The development server revealed two additional warnings: React list-key warnings on Safety and a local-origin warning. I’m fixing those now. One test also used Windows/Linux’s new-tab shortcut on macOS; I’ll make that test use the correct shortcut for either platform.

Reduced-motion testing found a hydration mismatch: the server and browser chose different initial animation styles. I’ve made the initial render consistent, then applied the browser’s motion preference. I’m checking both motion settings across all four pages.

The list-key, local-origin, and hydration warnings are resolved. All four pages pass the new checks with both motion settings. I’m finishing the regression run; development testing also exposed a test timing issue where keyboard input could arrive before the page finished loading.

The final build, lint, and TypeScript checks pass. Compiled CSS is still identical, and the full production test run is passing so far, including responsive layouts and animations.

Fixed the React key warnings, reduced-motion hydration errors, local-origin warning, and PostCSS vulnerabilities.

UI/UX preserved: compiled CSS is identical, and all 54 tests pass. Build, lint, and TypeScript checks also pass.

Production dependencies have zero reported vulnerabilities. Five development-only alerts remain from one [unpatched upstream issue](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vfj7-8cjw-p6xm).

messages.text:
You are working on an existing website deployed on Vercel (https://waabi-safety-reconstruction.vercel.app/). It is a university report website for the EWB Challenge 2026 project "Provisions Point" for Lama Lama Country. It has 4 pages: / (Overview), /safety (Solution), /company (Project), /careers (Delivery).

GOAL
Build ONE new single page at the route /report that contains all the report sections listed below, in that exact order. The 4 existing pages must stay UNTOUCHED so we can borrow and reuse their UI elements.

HARD RULES
1. Do NOT edit, delete, move or rename any existing page, component, style, asset or config for /, /safety, /company or /careers. Do not add redirects. Do not change the existing nav, header or footer. Only add new files, plus the smallest possible change needed to register the new route. Reuse existing components by importing them. If a component must change for the new page, make a copy with a new name and change the copy.
2. Reuse the existing UI (hero, cards, tabs, carousels, stat cards, tiles, CTA, footer, fonts, colours, spacing, animation) so the new page looks like the same site. Do not add new libraries. Put any new CSS in new, scoped files so existing pages cannot change.
3. Do not rewrite, shorten, reword or fix any copy. Copy our assignment text exactly as it is on the old pages. Only change a heading when this prompt says so.
4. IRRELEVANT CONTENT: where a reused UI element would show content that is not our assignment content (template videos, the hero image strip, logo tiles or logo marquee, any image whose alt text starts with "Placeholder image", "Flat monogram tile" images, stock template photos), keep the UI element and show the exact text (change to our assignment content) in its place. Do not remove the element. Do not fix or judge it. Images whose alt text starts "Concept image" stay as they are. The two matrix screenshot images stay as they are.
5. Build the new page with its own header: a copy of the existing header with an anchor nav (Summary, Background, Options, Design, Prototype, Delivery, Cost, References, Appendices). Smooth scroll, offset for the fixed header, highlight the active section on scroll. All links on the new page are in-page anchors using the section ids below. The new page needs its own footer copy with the same rule.
6. BEFORE inserting any placeholder, search the whole codebase (components, content files, JSON, markdown, tab and carousel data) for that content. If it exists, use it. Only insert a placeholder if it exists nowhere.
7. PLACEHOLDER SPEC (exact): a div with the section id, width 100%, height 20vh, background #ffffff, no border, no shadow, no border radius, display flex, content centred both ways, black text, containing only the text: insert: <section name>. Nothing else.
8. Keep every note that says "TEAM TO ADD" exactly as written. Give them a yellow highlight background on the new page so they are visible. Do not remove them.
9. Do not write em dashes in any new text.
10. Duplicates: on the new page show only ONE copy of the project stages carousel (in Implementation Plan), ONE copy of the key numbers (2 m, 22 weeks, 220, in the Executive Summary), and ONE call to action and footer (at the bottom).
11. Exceptions to rule 2: on the new page, Table 1 and the reference list must be shown in full, with no pager or carousel. Build simple new components for these.

HEADING FIXES (new page only, do not change the old pages)
- Project page "Organisations and sources in this proposal": call the tile row "Stakeholders and organisations". Move its paragraph "Visitors and experience." to Background.
- Project page "Project stages": move its paragraph "Tourism economy and maintenance." to Background.
- The Project page hero text starting "The design must lower the risk of vehicles becoming stranded..." is Criterion 1, Safety and access. Move it to Design Criteria.

SECTION ORDER (each section is an element with the id shown, plus an H2 heading)

0. Header (own header with anchor nav) and hero. Hero title "Provisions Point", tagline "A proposed supply and recovery shelter for Lama Lama Country." Hero media: (change to our assignment content).

1. id="title-block", "Cover details". Source: the home tab block "Context / Opportunity / Cover / How might we". Show as a labelled list: Website title, Design Area, Project Opportunity, How Might We statement, Tutorial number and zone, Group name. Use whatever exists. For any missing fields add one placeholder: insert: Tutorial number and zone, group name.

2. id="summary", "Executive Summary", in this order:
   a. the line "EWB Challenge 2026 | Design Opportunity 2.1"
   b. placeholder: insert: Keywords
   c. H3 "Proposal Summary": the home paragraph starting "The project aims to give visitors..."
   d. H3 "Overview of design": the home Overview of design text, the purchased materials list and its two concept images
   e. the key numbers (2 m, 22 weeks, 220) using the existing stat card UI. Card background media: (change to our assignment content). No links.
   f. placeholder: insert: Key Considerations
   g. H3 "Proposed Materials and Cost Summary": the home Purchased / Other / Total tabs. If Other or Total has no content, add placeholder: insert: Estimated total cost (AUD)

3. id="group-declaration", "Group Declaration". From The team text, build a 2-column table (Group Member Name, Project Contributions) with 6 rows: Pinhong, Darrell, Tasneef, Isaac, Jude, Qijun. Copy each contribution exactly. Member image tiles: (change to our assignment content).

4. id="acknowledgement", "Team Acknowledgement". Source: home Acknowledgement of Country, with its TEAM TO ADD note. Side image: (change to our assignment content).

5. id="project-details", "Project details": home "Why this project matters", the Context tab text, the Opportunity tab text, then the "Stakeholders and organisations" tiles using the existing tile UI, one tile per name, each name shown once as text: Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation, Lama Lama Rangers, Engineers Without Borders Australia, University of Technology Sydney, Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service, Cook Shire Council, Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation, National Indigenous Australians Agency.

6. id="background", "Background", H3s in this order: Climate and flooding; Existing infrastructure and safety (both from the Project hero); Visitors and experience; Tourism economy and maintenance; Cultural values and protocols (from the Project page "Background"). Then two placeholders: insert: Ecological and environmental values, and insert: Current practices and existing solutions, and why they are not enough. Keep the flood and aerial concept images with their alt text.

7. id="problem", placeholder: insert: Problem Description (user needs statement)

8. id="criteria", "Design Criteria": Criterion 1 Safety and access (moved from the Project hero), then Criteria 2, 3 and 4 from the Project criteria carousel, in number order, using the existing criteria card UI. Then one placeholder: insert: Design Criteria: Culture and Country, Low cost, Community fit, Revenue. If any of these four exist in the code, use them and list only the missing ones.

9. id="options", "Design solution options": Solution page "Design options" intro, the screened-out beacon note, Option A, Option B, Option C.

10. id="selection", "Design Selection": "How the team chose", both matrix images with their text, "Reading the scores", and the Decision line.

11. id="design", "Detailed Design": "Why it should work" and the "Note on the 2 m height" text (without the repeated key numbers), then the 4 slides in order: What it is; Entry, stock and hire items; How a visitor would use it; Community concerns. Put the abstract site plan figure (map.svg) after "What it is".

12. id="prototyping", placeholder: insert: Prototyping

13. id="implementation", "Implementation Plan": the Delivery "Implementation plan" list and "Community, ownership and evaluation" block, then the project stages carousel with the home heading "Project stages." and its intro line, plus the sentence "The design is a student proposal. It is for the Yintjingga Aboriginal Corporation to review, change or reject."

14. id="cost", "Cost Analysis": Table 1 "Build and stock cost (AUD)" with all 16 rows visible and its caption. Do not copy the empty duplicate "What it costs" heading. Then placeholder: insert: Revenue projections and funding sources (only if not found in the code).

15. id="other", "Other considerations": the Delivery "Other considerations" block (stakeholders, visitor journey, ranger journey, community reaction, wider issues).

16. id="recommendations", "Recommendations": the "What should happen next" text.

17. id="references", "References": all 26 entries as one plain alphabetical list, same wording.

18. id="appendices", "Supporting documentation", in this order:
   Appendix 1: Group charter (keep the TEAM TO ADD line, add placeholder: insert: Appendix 1: Group charter)
   Appendix 2: Meeting minutes (keep the note, add placeholder: insert: Appendix 2: Meeting minutes)
   Appendix 3: Statement of AI use and prompt log (existing text and note, then placeholder: insert: Appendix 3: Prompt screenshots)
   Appendix 4: Full prototype test results (keep the note, add placeholder: insert: Appendix 4: Prototype test results)
   Appendix 5: Decision matrix and cost workings (existing text)

19. Bottom: a copy of the call to action ("Explore the problem, the solution and the plan to deliver it.") with the contact route TEAM TO ADD note, buttons linking to #summary and #implementation, then the footer copy with the Acknowledgement of Country link to #acknowledgement. Decorative media in the call to action: (change to our assignment content).

QUALITY
Run a production build with zero errors and zero console errors. Check /report at 375px, 768px and 1440px widths. No horizontal scroll, no broken anchors. Check that /, /safety, /company and /careers still look and work exactly as before.

WHEN DONE, REPLY WITH
- the new route and file list
- proof the old pages are untouched (git diff showing no changes to existing page or component files, other than route registration)
- the list of section ids in page order
- every placeholder inserted and every one skipped because the content was found
- every place where you used (change to our assignment content)

The new Overview of Design block now matches the original materials section. I checked it in the browser and compared screenshots of the two at the same scroll position.

**What was wrong:** My question-length subheadings were wrapping onto four lines each at the big tab font size. That made the tab column 670px tall, against 300px in the original, so the whole block looked off.

**The fix:** I shortened the subheadings so each fits on one line, and moved the full question into the text under each tab. These are the edits in the `overview` array in [page.tsx](waabi-safety-reconstruction/app/report/page.tsx).

| Subheading | Text under it |
|---|---|
| What and how? | What is the design, what does it aim to achieve and how does it work? `--------------` [30 words] |
| Supported by? | What supports the implementation of the design? `--------------` [25 words] |
| Components? | What physical components does the design include? `--------------` [30 words] |
| Who and why? | Who will use the design, and how and why will they use it? `--------------` [35 words] |

messages.text:
in the design option section change the content to this:
**3.1. Design option 1: Provisions Point **
The Provisions Point is a flood-resilient facility designed to provide visitors with essential supplies and emergency equipment during wet-season flooding. The proposed structure features an elevated platform, weather-resistant storage facilities, and secure compartments containing drinking water, non-perishable food, first-aid supplies, and vehicle recovery equipment. Personal Locator Beacons (PLBs) and UHF radios would also be available to support emergency communication. This solution aims to improve visitor safety and access to essential resources while creating potential revenue opportunities through equipment rental. 
**3.2. Design option 2: Elevated tent-site platform **
The Elevated Tent-site Platform proposes raised camping platforms designed to reduce visitors' exposure to ground-level flooding and wet conditions. The platforms would provide stable areas for setting up tents, potentially reducing damage to camping equipment and improving camping conditions during periods of heavy rainfall. 
This solution focuses primarily on providing a safer camping environment rather than supplying emergency resources. Its relatively simple design could reduce initial construction costs, while its elevated structure offers improved flood resilience compared with ground-level campsites. However, the platforms would provide limited access to emergency supplies, communication equipment, and vehicle recovery services. 
**3.3. Design option 3: Distributed emergency checkpoint **
The Distributed Emergency Checkpoint proposes a network of small emergency support stations positioned at selected locations around Warokutal. Each checkpoint could contain basic emergency supplies, safety information, and communication equipment, allowing visitors to access assistance without relying on a single central facility. 
By distributing emergency resources across multiple locations, this solution aims to improve accessibility and provide support to visitors who may become stranded during flooding. The stations could also be adapted to local environmental and community requirements.

1.1 The primary target audience for the project consists of independent travellers and managers of local tourism facilities that operate within Lama Lama country on the Cape York Peninsula. Historically, recurring wet season flooding severely damages unsealed roads, trapping travellers who lack adequate protection or backup emergency resources. 

 

1.2 We have selected Design Opportunity 2.1, Resilient visitor infrastructure, this project focuses on Warokutal. The design provides an elevated, minimal maintenance supply point that supplies stranded visitors with dependable access to water, long shelf life rations, radios and PLBs, and vehicle recovery equipment.

messages.text:
in the decisions solutions page change the content to these for each solution:
**Design option 1: Provisions Point **
The Provisions Point is a small, raised building that stocks drinking water, non-perishable food, first-aid supplies and vehicle recovery gear. Visitors can also hire personal locator beacons (PLBs) and UHF radios to call for help. It is aimed at visitors caught out by wet-season flooding, and it earns income through sales and hire. 

This option suits Warokutal because it can be built on ground that has already been cleared. No new vegetation needs to be removed, and visitors are kept away from culturally restricted areas such as the Alingina Wungku Living Area (Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service [QPWS], 2013). Its main drawbacks are cost and workload. It is the most expensive of the three options to build, and it adds a restocking task for Rangers, who already handle tourism and repairs on top of their other work (Reardon-Smith, 2023). 

**Design option 2: Elevated tent-site platform **
The Elevated Tent-site Platform would raise camping areas off the ground so that tents and gear stay dry during heavy rain. It is simple and fairly cheap to build, and the raised decks handle flooding well. However, it does nothing for visitors who are stranded, as it offers no supplies, communication or vehicle recovery. Building several platforms would also spread construction across the campground, and each one would need checking by Rangers after every wet season. 

**Design option 3: Distributed emergency checkpoint **
The Distributed Emergency Checkpoint would place several small stations around Warokutal, each with basic supplies, safety information and a radio, so that visitors are not relying on one central building. 

Having stations in several places could mean a stranded visitor has less distance to travel for help. The downside is that each station would need its own approval to make sure it avoids culturally and environmentally sensitive areas (QPWS, 2013). Keeping several sites stocked would also add to the Rangers’ workload. The stations would be too small to hold vehicle recovery gear, and they would bring in little or no income for the community.

** Detailed Design **
The Provisions Point is a small building of about 24 m² at Warokutal (Safari Camp), placed on already-cleared, higher ground within the campground. It is staffed by Lama Lama Rangers during the visitor season (July to November). 

**7.1 Structure** 
The building is raised 2 m on reinforced concrete piles so that floodwater can pass underneath. The walls are watertight concrete, which protects the steel reinforcement inside, and the roof is corrugated fibre cement, which handles heavy rain, strong sun and cyclone winds with very little upkeep. Shallow pile footings are used instead of deep trenches to limit digging on Country. A small solar panel and battery power the lighting and charge the radios and beacons, so no generator or fuel is needed. 

**7.2 What it holds** 
 Shelves and a counter hold drinking water, canned food, firewood, first-aid supplies and safety flyers. Two vehicle recovery kits are available for hire, each with traction boards, a tyre deflation kit, a 12V compressor, and a snatch strap with shackles. Personal locator beacons (PLBs) and UHF radios can also be hired, so visitors can contact Rangers in areas with no phone reception. A small emergency cabinet stocked with water and a UHF radio is opened with a code given at check-in, so help is available even when no Ranger is on site. 

**7.3 How it works** 
A visitor checks in, buys supplies or hires gear, and returns it before leaving the area. Rangers restock weekly during the season and inspect the building twice a year, before and after the wet season. Sales and hire income covers running costs (see Cost Analysis).

Objective of the prototype page:
Prototypes have two purposes:
• To show your audience what the design looks like.
• To test whether the design or an aspect of the design will work.
Much of this section should be figures/tables or pictures.
Each team is expected to make at least one prototype and should detail the processes, the prototype,
and the testing of the prototype.
Briefly detail:
- How did you identified what should be prototyped and why.
- How you constructed the prototype.
- What the prototype looks like and what it can do.
- How you tested the prototype.
- The results of the testing, including any modifications you have made.
Detailed test and evaluation results as well as additional large images or other relevant information
can be provided in the Appendices. However, these should be briefly referred to on your website to
inform the reader of the information and its significance (e.g., The full test results are provided in
Appendix 2 for reference).

Final content of prototype page, (image attached) and text below, dont change anything:
Purpose 

The prototype was made to show what the Provisions Point would look like and to check that its layout works in the space available. 

 

How it was built 

The model was built in Blender. AI was used to generate basic shapes quickly, which were then arranged, resized and assembled into the building. The model uses the same materials as the design: reinforced concrete piles, watertight concrete walls and a corrugated fibre cement roof, on elevated ground. 

  

Testing 

The model was used to check that the layout is logical, that the building’s size stays within budget, and that the recovery kits and supplies fit on the shelves and counter. 

 

The model showed that the building is well supported and sits on higher ground, so it is unlikely to be damaged by floods. The roof sits flush against the walls, and the size of the building matches the cost estimate. The recovery gear and supplies fit inside, although they were modelled simply and are hard to make out in the images. A more detailed model of the interior would be the next step. 
<image name=[Image #1] path="[proto-1.png]"></image><image name=[Image #2] path="[proto-2.png]"></image><image name=[Image #3] path="[proto-3.png]"></image><image name=[Image #4] path="[proto-4.png]"></image>

I’ll inspect the current prototype section and your four images, then suggest a clearer layout while keeping all your text unchanged.

I’d use a **visual walkthrough**: show the whole building first, then the interior, then explain the testing. The current prototype page is a placeholder, so this would give it a clear structure while keeping your text exactly as supplied.

### Suggested layout

**1. Purpose + main exterior image**

Use two columns:

- **Left, about one third:** “Purpose” and its paragraph.
- **Right, about two thirds:** **Image 2**, shown large.

Image 2 is the clearest introduction because readers can immediately see the building, raised supports and access ramp. Keep the page title compact so the model appears near the top.

**2. How it was built + second exterior view**

Place **Image 3 on the left** and “How it was built” with its paragraph on the right.

This angle shows the building’s depth and supporting piles. Placing it beside the construction explanation helps readers connect the materials and structure to the model.

**3. Interior images**

Show the two interior views together:

- **Image 4 larger:** gives readers an overview of the room and its arrangement.
- **Image 1 smaller:** provides a closer look at the shelves and supplies.

Use approximately a **60/40 split**, with both images displayed at the same height. Avoid cropping away useful details.

**4. Testing**

Keep the existing “Testing” heading, followed by:

- The first paragraph as the introduction.
- The final paragraph beneath it in a softly shaded panel, making the findings and next step easy to locate.

Keep that final paragraph intact. Its last two sentences already explain the model’s limitation and the next step.

```text
Prototype

Purpose                  [ Image 2: main exterior ]
[exact paragraph]

[ Image 3: exterior ]    How it was built
                         [exact paragraph]

[ Image 4: interior overview ] [ Image 1: shelves ]

Testing
```

## 1.1 The context of your project

The primary target audience for the project consists of independent travellers and managers of local tourism facilities that operate within Lama Lama country on the Cape York Peninsula. Warokutal (Safari Camp) is a remote campground at Port Stewart, reached by roads that can become impassable in the wet season, so the national park is typically closed from 1 December to 30 June (DETSI, 2024a). The park offers remote, low-key, self-reliant visitor experiences (QPWS, 2013), but the Ranger Base is staffed only from about 8 am to 4:30 pm and campground water is non-potable (YAC, n.d.). Visitors who get stuck can be left without water, supplies or a way to call for help, which is why this project matters. \


## 1.2 Why is this important?

\
For local tourism facility managers and rangers, the project addresses a critical operational gap. By establishing a durable supply point, the facility aims to reduce recurring emergency repair expenses and minimises the need for high-risk ranger interventions during flooding seasons’ extreme weather events. The project ultimately bridges the gap between the risks associated with tourism and wet season flooding, ensuring visitors can manage unexpected weather disruptions while safeguarding Lama Lama’s cultural and environmental assets. 



## 1.3 Which Design Area and Project Opportunity (Topic) has your group selected?

\
This project responds to Design Area 2, Eco-tourism and Visitor Experience, and Design Opportunity 2.1, Resilient visitor infrastructure, and focuses on Warokutal. The design is an elevated, low maintenance supply point that gives stranded visitors dependable access to water, long shelf-life food, radios, PLBs and vehicle recovery equipment. \


## 1.4 What is your needs statement?

\
The needs statement is that visitors to Warokutal need dependable access to water, supplies, recovery equipment and a way to call for help when roads are damaged, without adding to the workload of the Rangers.

**7. Detailed Design **



The Provisions Point is a small building of about 24 m² at Warokutal (Safari Camp), placed on already-cleared, higher ground within the campground. It is staffed by Lama Lama Rangers during the visitor season (July to November). 

**7.1 Structure** \
The building is raised 2 m on reinforced concrete piles so that floodwater can pass underneath. The walls are watertight concrete, which protects the steel reinforcement inside, and the roof is corrugated fibre cement, which handles heavy rain, strong sun and cyclone winds with very little upkeep. Shallow pile footings are used instead of deep trenches to limit digging on Country. A small solar panel and battery power the lighting and charge the radios and beacons, so no generator or fuel is needed. 



**7.2 What it holds** \
Shelves and a counter hold drinking water, canned food, firewood, first-aid supplies and safety flyers. Two vehicle recovery kits are available for hire, each with traction boards, a tyre deflation kit, a 12V compressor, and a snatch strap with shackles. Personal locator beacons (PLBs) and UHF radios can also be hired, so visitors can contact Rangers in areas with no phone reception. A small emergency cabinet stocked with water and a UHF radio is opened with a code given at check-in, so help is available even when no Ranger is on site. 



**7.3 How it works** \
A visitor checks in, buys supplies or hires gear, and returns it before leaving the area. Rangers restock weekly during the season and inspect the building twice a year, before and after the wet season. Sales and hire income covers running costs (see Cost Analysis). 

**7.4 Community concerns** 

- The likely concerns and how the design addresses them: 

* Damage to Country: The building is on already-cleared ground, and its placement is agreed with Traditional Owners first. 

- Extra Ranger work: Rangers restock weekly in the season, and hire income covers running costs. 

* Flood damage: The building is raised 2 m, with flood heights confirmed before construction. 

- Unsafe wet-season travel: The park stays closed from 1 December to 30 June (DETSI, 2024a), and the building is for stranded visitors. 

* Misuse of hire gear: Gear is checked on return and repaired or replaced.

**5. Design solution options **
The team developed three options in response to the design problem. Each was looked at in terms of what it would mean for visitors, the Lama Lama Rangers and Traditional Owners. A fourth idea, a solar-powered beacon showing river crossing conditions, was also considered. It scored lowest in the decision matrix, so it is not covered in detail here. 

**Design option 1: Provisions Point **
The Provisions Point is a small, raised building that stocks drinking water, non-perishable food, first-aid supplies and vehicle recovery gear. Visitors can also hire personal locator beacons (PLBs) and UHF radios to call for help. It is aimed at visitors caught out by wet-season flooding, and it earns income through sales and hire. 

This option suits Warokutal because it can be built on ground that has already been cleared. No new vegetation needs to be removed, and visitors are kept away from culturally restricted areas such as the Alingina Wungku Living Area (Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service [QPWS], 2013). Its main drawbacks are cost and workload. It is the most expensive of the three options to build, and it adds a restocking task for Rangers, who already handle tourism and repairs on top of their other work.. 

**Design option 2: Elevated tent-site platform **
The Elevated Tent-site Platform would raise camping areas off the ground so that tents and gear stay dry during heavy rain. It is simple and fairly cheap to build, and the raised decks handle flooding well. However, it does nothing for visitors who are stranded, as it offers no supplies, communication or vehicle recovery. Building several platforms would also spread construction across the campground, and each one would need checking by Rangers after every wet season. 

**Design option 3: Distributed emergency checkpoint **
The Distributed Emergency Checkpoint would place several small stations around Warokutal, each with basic supplies, safety information and a radio, so that visitors are not relying on one central building. 

Having stations in several places could mean a stranded visitor has less distance to travel for help. The downside is that each station would need its own approval to make sure it avoids culturally and environmentally sensitive areas (QPWS, 2013). Keeping several sites stocked would also add to the Rangers’ workload. The stations would be too small to hold vehicle recovery gear, and they would bring in little or no income for the community.

2. **Background **

2.1 Lama Lama Country is located on the eastern coast of the Cape York Peninsula, Queensland. The region experiences a tropical monsoon climate that is characterised by wet and dry seasons. Between October and April, the land experiences heavy and extensive rainfall, where historical data showed that early wet season (October to December) experiences concentrated precipitation that acts as a catalyst for sudden flash flooding (Bureau of Meteorology, 2018). This impacts unsealed roads that connect remote camping areas such as Warokutal and Maramba and isolate visitors from external emergency services.  

2.2 The landscape holds profound spiritual, historical and cultural significance for the Lama Lama Traditional Owners, who manage the region alongside the Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service (QPWS, 2013). Because travel through the national park and surrounding areas is restricted as it is culturally and environmentally sensitive, any infrastructure intervention must respect sacred sites and minimise ecological disruption.  

2.3 Furthermore, since regional infrastructure is traditionally maintained reactively rather than proactively, leaving remote sites vulnerable to severe weathering damage, the aim is to build something that needs to be maintained as little as possible. Currently, the Port Stewart Ranger Base serves as the primary safety outpost that is staffed, for the entire region, leaving remote camps exposed during weather emergencies. 

2.4 Rainfall in the early wet season (October to December) varies widely from year to year, which leads to flooding that is both widespread and sudden (Bureau of Meteorology, 2018). 



2.5 During the rainy season, buildings and equipment are susceptible to damage from flash floods and sudden downpours, necessitating significant capital for repairs before they can be used again for tourism. For visitors, the lack of any nearby shelter or supply point makes emergencies extremely hard to manage. 



2.6 Camping is currently kept outside the national park boundary, at the nearby campgrounds of Warokutal and Maramba (DETSI, 2024a). There is no alternative to visitors bringing their own recovery equipment. The Ranger Base at Port Stewart is currently the only staffed safety point for the whole area. 



2.7 The project aims to improve visitors’ access to essential supplies at Warokutal (Safari Camp), particularly when wet-season flooding disrupts road access. It seeks to develop an affordable, flood-resilient solution that reduces maintenance and repair demands on rangers. The design should minimise disturbance to the surrounding environment and protect culturally significant areas. Consultation with Traditional Owners should guide the design and its implementation to ensure that the proposed solution respects community need and cultural values.

Design Area 2 – Eco-tourism and Visitor Experience; Opportunity 2.1 – Resilient visitor infrastructure 

**Keywords:** Visitor security, flood resilience, remote infrastructure, emergency supplies, vehicle recovery. 

**Proposal Summary  **

This project aims to give visitors to Warokutal (Safari Camp) access to water, supplies and vehicle recovery equipment when floods damage the roads. It proposes an elevated, minimal maintenance shelter that stocks essentials and hires out recovery kits, personal locator beacons and ultra high frequency radios. 

**Overview of Design **

The design improves flood resilience and supply security through an elevated, low-maintenance building staffed by Lama Lama Rangers during the visitor season, with a small emergency cabinet available at all times. 

The implementation of this design is supported through durable, low-maintenance materials, local community partnerships to aid with stocking and maintenance, and clear signage guiding users when flooding occurs. 

The building sits 2 m above ground on reinforced concrete piles, with watertight concrete walls and a corrugated fibre cement roof. It stocks drinking water, non-perishable food, firewood and first-aid supplies, and hires out vehicle recovery kits, personal locator beacons and UHF radios. A small solar system powers the lighting and charges the radios and beacons. 



Visitors, Traditional Owners and Rangers travelling through Warokutal will use this facility, either during or immediately after severe floods when unsealed roads become unusable, stranding travellers without immediate access to rescue services. 

**Key Considerations **

- Where are the recommended materials sourced from? (i.e. externally or locally available) 

Reinforced concrete piles, watertight concrete and corrugated fibre cement sheeting, chosen for their resistance to flooding, termites, corrosion and cyclone winds. Materials will be sourced from regional suppliers and delivered during the dry season. 



- What are the key maintenance requirements? 

Rangers restock weekly during the visitor season (July to November) and carry out two inspections a year, before and after the wet season. Hire gear is checked on return, and damaged items are repaired or replaced. Structural or electrical faults are handled by qualified contractors. 



- How do you propose the design might be implemented? 

1. Community consultation with Lama Lama Traditional Owners and local land councils to finalise placement and cultural protocols. 

2) Dry season construction by a crew of four, taking about eight weeks. 

3. A four hour training session for Rangers, with an instruction manual kept on site. 

- What additional consultation/feedback/research might be required to validate your design proposal? What might the next steps be to make this idea happen? 

Conduct flood-height assessments with Traditional Owners to confirm the right building height. Seek YAC approval, which takes about six months.
